1:
The pursuit resumes the moment the foreign war is over. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks the ingratitude: no sooner had Saul come home safely from chasing the Philistines than he enquired after David to do him a mischief; and it is not enough for Saul that David is cooped up, for he cannot be easy while he is alive. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the size of the force as a measure of the fear behind it: three thousand chosen men show how thoroughly Saul was impressed with David’s power, looking on him as a rival king; and the Ziphites, who knew the passes of that barren region, were ready to guide him.

The phrase that names the place is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold that the rocks of the wild goats is probably no proper name but a general term for the rocks of that locality, from the number of wild goats and chamois found all over the region. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports the versions at variance: the Vulgate paraphrases them as the most precipitous rocks over which the ibexes alone can travel, the Targum makes them the caverns of the rocks, and the Greek turns the phrase into a proper name, evidently a corruption of the Hebrew. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds that the rocks are exceeding steep and dangerous to travellers, as an eye-witness has left on record, and yet Saul was so transported with rage as to venture himself and his army there.

What Saul went into the cave to do is disputed harder. Clarke takes it of easing nature, with the Vulgate, the Greek, the Targum and the Arabic, after which he lay down to repose; and he relays the rabbinic conceit that God caused a spider to weave her web over the cave’s mouth, so that Saul took it for granted no one had lately been there, calling it one of the most elegant in their whole collection. Henry allows that reading but prefers sleep, and Wesley argues it from the man: Saul was a soldier used to sleeping on the ground and, weary with incessant marching, both needed and desired rest, God so disposing him that David might have this occasion to demonstrate his integrity. Ellicott calls the simple sense enough: fatigued with the morning’s march he withdrew about midday for a siesta, and an attendant threw the royal mantle lightly over the king’s feet; the other reading by no means suits the narrative, since time was needed for a sentinel to inform David and for David to approach, cut the hem, and retire.

What the men claimed as a promise is rejected. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the words might refer to an oracle received through a prophet, but hold that what follows shows David had received none: the men treated the leadings of providence as a divine intimation and called that a word of Jehovah. Henry turns it into a double warning: God had assured David he would deliver him from Saul, and his men read that as a warrant to destroy Saul; and because it was in his power to kill him they concluded he might lawfully do it. Clarke goes further than the others, judging from the circumstances that David rose intending to take Saul’s life, and was prevented only by the remonstrance of God in his conscience. Ellicott has him listen to the tempter for a moment only, until there passed through his soul the thought that the helpless sleeping one was the anointed of Jehovah, and that he, himself an anointed king, could not touch another of the same order to do him harm.
5:
Why the conscience struck is this pericope’s question. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says it was not for what David had done to Saul but for the momentary thought that had stained his soul, of slaying the Lord’s anointed; he prefers this to the view of Clericus, that David feared Saul would take the sign in bad part, and holds there is no sign at all of David’s regretting that he cut the fringe. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the opposite view, that his conscience reproached him because he regarded the cutting itself as an injury done to the king. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) stands with them: though it did Saul no real hurt, and served David afterwards for proof that it had been in his power to kill him, because it was an affront to royal dignity he wished he had not done it. John Gill (reformed) puts it plainly, that his conscience accused him and he repented of what he had done. Henry draws the general lesson, that it is a good thing to have a heart within us smiting us for sins that seem little, since it is a sign that conscience is awake and tender and will prevent greater sins. Ellicott notes that the act was severely judged elsewhere, a rabbi reading the cutting of the robe as the slighting of clothes that would one day leave David himself unwarmed by them — one of those cryptographs, he says, whose real lesson is reverence for the guides of Israel, here represented by Saul.

The ground of the refusal is the anointing. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) holds that however unworthily Saul was acting, he had been appointed to his office by God and could be removed only by the authority that placed him there; David grounds his forbearance on just that, since Saul is his master and he the subject, and the Lord’s anointed is sacred as to his person in the Lord’s sight. It is an awful thing to kill a king, he adds, even the most untoward, once constitutionally appointed; no experiment of the kind has ever succeeded, and had David taken away Saul’s life he would in God’s sight have been a murderer. Henry notices what David refused to consider: not Saul as his enemy, the one man standing in the way of his preferment, for then he would have been induced to hearken to the temptation, but Saul as God’s anointed, under the particular protection of the divine law, and as his master, to whom he owed faithfulness. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the firmness of the refusal itself shows clearly enough that no word of Jehovah had come to him to do as he liked with Saul.

Restraining the men is counted a second act. Clarke makes it a duty rather than a kindness: as he could restrain them it was his duty to do so, and had he connived at their killing him David would have been the murderer; he adds that in praying for the king we call God the only Ruler of princes, their authority being the highest among men and next to God’s own, and quotes the poet that kings are supreme over their subjects while Jove is supreme over kings. Henry presses the double refusal: he would not do this evil thing himself, nor suffer those about him to do it, and thus rendered good for evil to the man from whom he had received evil for good, being herein both a type of Christ, who saved his persecutors, and an example to all Christians to overcome evil with good. Gill reports the manner with the Targum, that he pacified them and made them easy in his not having slain the king, reconciling their minds by observing that Saul was the anointed of the Lord.
8:
The appeal opens with homage. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) has the outlaw let the king proceed some little way before calling after him, with an address of the deepest reverence and an act of the profoundest homage an inferior could pay a superior: he would show Saul at least that he was no rival king. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that he called out so that, when the king looked round, he might expostulate with him in words at once reverent and earnest, sharpening his conscience as to the unfounded nature of his suspicion. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) finds courage in the mere showing of his head, since David had reason to think Saul would be the death of him as soon as he saw him, yet he laid that jealousy aside and bowed, teaching us to order ourselves reverently even to superiors who have injured us.

Blaming the counsellors rather than the king is read as tact. Henry calls it a piece of respect due to crowned heads, if they do amiss, to charge it upon those about them, and notes that David had reason enough to think Saul persecuted him purely from his own envy, yet courteously supposes that others put him on to it. Ellicott supplies the men: David had many deadly enemies at court who laboured with success to deepen Saul’s jealousy, Doeg among the most prominent, another the Benjamite named in the title of the seventh psalm, with the Ziphites represented there too. John Gill (reformed) sees the purpose: David laid the blame on the courtiers rather than on Saul the rather to reconcile him and make him willing to listen.

The word father and the piece of cloth carry the proof. Ellicott denies that father here means father-in-law, since the king’s daughter had probably already been given to another man; it is simply the reverence of the young to the old, of the loyal subject to the sovereign. Gill keeps both senses, a father naturally as having married his daughter and civilly as a king who ought to have been the father of his country. Henry puts the evidence at its sharpest: had the charge been true he would now have had Saul’s head in his hand and not the skirt of his robe, for he could as easily have cut off the one as the other. Ellicott adds that one clause is a crux, since the literal rendering would make Jehovah himself bid David kill — defended by some who treat God’s allowing Saul to choose that cavern as a direction to slay him, though the English rightly follows the Syriac and Chaldee in supplying some, or better one.

The proverb and the two similes close the speech. Keil and Delitzsch give its force in a sentence, that only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself, and David does not. Ellicott gathers the same from Clericus and Grotius, that actions usually correspond to the quality of the mind, and adds the Greek proverb that from a bad raven comes a bad egg; Gill asks instead whose proverb it is, reporting Kimchi for the first man and the Talmud for the Ancient of days. Henry allows a second sense, that men’s own iniquity will ruin them at last, and draws the rule that though wickedness proceed from the wicked it must not proceed from us by way of retaliation, since though the dog bark at the sheep the sheep does not bark at the dog. On the similes Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes that a dead dog was a term of the most sovereign contempt, the Targum rendering both figures as one weak and one contemptible, and Ellicott observes that the original is stronger still, a single flea, which is not easily caught and if caught is poor game for a royal hunter.
16:
That the king heard the speech out is the first wonder. John Gill (reformed) finds it wonderful that Saul, so eager for David’s life, should stand still and not fall upon him, and ascribes it to the restraining providence of God, to his surprise at David coming out of the cave, and above all to the skirt in his hand, a sure token that his life had been spared. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) agrees that God restrained him, supposes Saul struck with amazement at the singularity of the event, and says his heart must have been harder than a stone if this had not affected him. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the address as the measure of the change: David had called Saul his master, lord and king, and Saul accosts him as his son, to show he wished to receive him as formerly into his family.

How far the confession goes is measured exactly. Henry holds that he should have said, Thou art righteous but I am wicked, whereas the utmost he will own is that David is the more righteous; bad men commonly go no further, allowing that others are better than they. Many mourn for their sins, he adds, who do not truly repent of them, weeping bitterly yet continuing in league with them. Gill reaches the same verdict: Saul still thought himself righteous, and though David’s righteousness was so glaring that his enemy himself being judge acknowledged it, he would not confess his own wickedness, having no true sense of sin.

What made Saul certain of David’s accession is canvassed four ways. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reports Clericus, that from such magnanimity Saul concluded a man so superior in soul to kings could not but reign, and calls it a good comment with more behind it: Saul had never forgotten Samuel’s word that the kingdom was rent from him and given to a better neighbour, whom the son of Jesse’s bright career seemed to point out. Gill adds a token: the cutting of the skirt might have recalled the rending of Samuel’s mantle, with a Jewish tradition that Samuel had told him the man who cut off his skirt should reign after him. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) judge the wish perfectly sincere, David’s behaviour having conquered for the moment the evil demon of his heart; the conviction had long forced itself upon him, and drove the persecution whenever the evil spirit had the upper hand. Clarke states the indictment in a line: he knew this before, and yet pursued him with the most deadly hatred.

The oath and the parting show a man securing his name but not his soul. Ellicott explains the request from the practice of the jealous East, where a new dynasty commonly destroyed the fallen house — a fate Jonathan had dreaded enough to write into his own covenant with David. Clarke notes the asymmetry: Saul knew an oath would bind David though it had not bound himself, having sworn to Jonathan that David should not be slain and yet sought by every means to destroy him. Henry observes that David had the better claim to such an oath and did not press it, and that Saul, who had ruined his own soul and never took care to prevent that ruin, was nonetheless very solicitous that his name should not be cut off. Gill follows the keeping of it, in the sparing of Mephibosheth and the punishing of Ishbosheth’s murderers. Henry closes on the parting: Saul went home convinced but not converted, ashamed of his envy yet keeping that root of bitterness, and God has many ways to tie the hands of persecutors when he does not turn their hearts. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says David would trust him no more, having had frequent experience of his inconstancy.
